title: Sonu Nigam Packs Melbourne's Rod Laver Arena as 10,000 Fans Sing Along
excerpt: The Bollywood legend's first show at Melbourne's largest indoor arena — a three-act Revolution Tour set mixing romance, dance and classics — drew three generations of the diaspora alongside non-Indian Australians.
body:
• Sonu Nigam performed to a packed, 10,000-strong audience at Melbourne's Rod Laver Arena on October 10, 2026, as part of his multi-city Revolution Tour of Australia and New Zealand.
  • The set unfolded in three acts — romantic melodies, high-energy dance numbers including "All Is Well" and "Jeene Ke Hain Chaar Din," and a closing run of classics such as "Saathiya" and "Satrangi Re," alongside tributes to Kishore Kumar and Bappi Lahiri.
  • The crowd spanned three generations: first-generation migrants who grew up on these hits, their Australian-born children, and non-Indian Australians drawn by Nigam's vocal command.
  • The tour continues to Brisbane (Oct 11), Adelaide (Oct 16) and Perth (Oct 18), with tickets priced from AUD 79 via AXS and the tour promoter.

When the lights dimmed at Rod Laver Arena on Saturday, October 10, the first notes from Sonu Nigam's mouth fell over a packed house of 10,000 — and for the next two hours Melbourne stopped being a city and became a chorus. The Bollywood playback legend's stop on The Revolution Tour, presented by Desai Entertainment, was his first-ever performance at Melbourne's largest indoor arena, and the crowd treated it like the occasion it was.

The set unfolded in three acts. The first was romance: slow melodies that let the audience settle into the voice and the mood. The second turned to dance — "Jeene Ke Hain Chaar Din" had the hall on its feet, and "All Is Well" from 3 Idiots turned thousands of people into one cheerful chorus, the way it once did in cinemas across India. "Tu Aaja Soniye" and "Dil Mangta Hai Dildaar Soniye" sent dancers spilling into the aisles.

Nigam did not simply replay the records. He wove the hits together with medleys and fresh variations, and paid tribute to Kishore Kumar and Bappi Lahiri, the giants who shaped Hindi film music, reimagining their songs in his own idiom. The night's closing act was its cleverest move: after the frenzy, he brought the room gently back with "Saathiya," then kept the classics coming, among them "Satrangi Re" from Dil Se.

Fifty years of a voice

Nigam, 53, began singing at the age of four and in 2027 will mark 50 years of singing professionally — a rare milestone for any popular artist. His best-known recordings include "Sandese Aate Hain" from Border, the title song from Kal Ho Naa Ho, "Abhi Mujh Mein Kahin" from Agneepath and "Main Agar Kahoon" from Om Shanti Om, and he has sung in Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and English. For the migrants in Saturday's audience, those songs functioned as portable homelands — a single melody collapsing half a world in a second.

Three generations under one roof

What made the night unusual was not just the size of the crowd but its makeup. The estimated 10,000 who filled the hall included first-generation migrants who grew up on these hits, their Australian-born children who know them through playlists and their parents' car stereos, and a good number of non-Indian Australians who came out of curiosity and stayed for the sheer technical command of the singing — the range, the breath control, the ease across registers.

The show also reflected how far the Indian-Australian concert circuit has come. The production ran to the professional standards the venue demands, and Nigam's decision to play Rod Laver Arena signals that artists of his stature now treat Australia as a serious touring stop rather than an afterthought. That confidence took years of community organisations, venues, media outlets and steadily growing audiences to build. (The concert account this story is based on comes from The Australia Today, which was the tour's media partner and declared that stake.)

Soft power with a ticket price

There is a larger point worth making. Governments sign agreements and ministers exchange visits, but the India-Australia relationship is lived through evenings like this one: a Melbourne audience of 10,000, a commercially self-sustaining touring production, and a cultural exchange that works precisely because nobody pretends it is anything but entertainment. Melbourne has long treated culture as part of its civic life and its economy, not decoration — and Saturday night was the proof.

The tour rolls on

The Revolution Tour has already played Auckland's Spark Arena and Sydney's TikTok Entertainment Centre, and it heads next to Brisbane's Convention and Exhibition Centre on October 11, the Adelaide Entertainment Centre on October 16 and Perth's Riverside Theatre on October 18. Tickets are priced from AUD 79, available through AXS and the tour promoter.
